### A write set, a first effect contract: prove --writes refutes the setter that writes a protected field and proves its honest twin

change `qrqtplwqnrml` · [log `14c3eb3e4b95`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/9896d870-fb47-4f3c-ba4d-5b1d3e64719c/14c3eb3e4b95f2df5bcf919b4d77f270cb17c2f705aa95a9adf8675f63cdc58a.jsonl.gz)

The state stream's steps 4 and 5, the checking side. prove --writes this.displayName (own checker only) states which fields of a method's receiver and object parameters it may write. The check proves the frame with the property: after a normal return every other field of those inputs is unchanged, a primitive by value and a String or object by identity through the new p == \old(p) term. The frame is conjoined to the assertion, so a write outside the set is refuted by the harness and its witness runs on a JVM. Inside the call the engine refuses, by name, a write to anything else that existed before it: a static field, an array, an object no input is (even one a named field holds), or a class initialization, whose objects would look new to the call. This generalizes Engine::keeps through bmc::Options::frame. The cache refuses such a check, since its key does not read the write set.

### A library method the own checker can't run may be replaced by a stand-in sampled against it on a JVM (prove --stand-in), and a result that used one says it rests on it

change `qlylowvomrqr` · [log `e1a1803871d6`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/9896d870-fb47-4f3c-ba4d-5b1d3e64719c/e1a1803871d69a7a13d6b304bd99460f567e55864c83839c64064270d585332d.jsonl.gz)

Step 3, option 2, of the state stream's brief. Spring's bean wrapper resolves a property through its introspection caches and java.beans and calls the setter with Method.invoke, on every path of DataBinder.bind (example 286). Observing those caches is refused, and running them would need models of java.beans and java.lang.reflect. So the binding path gets a stand-in instead. Each public static method of the stand-in class (but main) replaces an instance method: its first parameter's class is the exact class of the receivers it covers, the rest of its descriptor is the method's. A call resolving to that method on a receiver of exactly that class runs the stand-in. A subclass's receiver, and the stand-in's own calls, run the method as written, so a stand-in hands back what it does not cover. Its main prints one line per sample with the method's outcome and the stand-in's. The tool runs it first on the check's class path and takes the stand-in only if every sample is the same, refusing it by the first input that differs, or when nothing is sampled, or for a public method that replaces nothing. A result that used a stand-in names it among what it rests on, with the number of samples, as sampled evidence and not a proof. A refutation through one is still replayed on a JVM. JBMC and --cache are refused.

Verified by lib/tests/stand_in.rs on the fixture lib/tests/fixtures/stand-ins, a reflective property writer. With the stand-in, a claim the method leaves undecided is proved and the stand-in is named; a refutation replays on a JVM. A subclass receiver, and a bean the stand-in hands back, stop at the method's gap as before. A stand-in that forgets 'Age', one that samples nothing, and one with a public helper are refused. Switching off the exact-receiver check, or the sample comparison, by mutation makes a test fail. test_costs run --changed passes, after the proof cache's projection named the new option. 286's own stand-in is drafted, not committed: sampled against 5.3.19's setPropertyValue, its 38,400 samples all match. Wiring it into the driver is the next cycle. The brief is not out of date.

**What it does.** `prove --writes this.displayName` says which fields of a method's receiver and object parameters the method may write. It works with `--engine native` only. The check then proves two things:
- **After the call:** every other field of those inputs is unchanged, compared by value or, for Strings and objects, by identity. This is added to the property's assertion, so a write outside the set comes back as an ordinary refutation whose witness replays on a JVM.
- **Inside the call:** the checker refuses any write to something else that existed before the call: a static field, an array, an object the inputs hold, or a class initialization. This extends `Engine::keeps`. The class-initialization case closes a gap I found while testing: objects an initializer makes during the call looked new, so writes to them would otherwise have passed.

**Results**, on a new fixture, `lib/tests/fixtures/claims/claims/Frames.java`:
- The brief's adversarial setter, which also writes `admin`, is refuted, and the witness replays on a JVM.

**Reply:**

I fixed a soundness hole in my own code this cycle, the one inbox item I008 reported. It is committed as `vvpxytqs`, and the commit check reported 0 errors. Nothing in example 286 is decided yet, and the frozen claim is unchanged.

**The bug:** under `--gaps assume`, an object that a JDK method returns was treated as being of exactly the class the method declares. So `HashSet.clone()` and `Date.clone()`, both declared to return `Object`, were "proved" to return no `HashSet` and no `Date`. A JVM says they do. My earlier refusal for this case (from inbox item I004) only caught an exact class match, so it missed these.

**The fix** (`lib/src/bmc/mod.rs`): such an object now has its declared class only when that class is final. Otherwise its real class is unknown (it could be any class below the declared one). Anything that depends on the real class is refused by name:
- calling a method on it, since a subclass's override may run;
- throwing it, since that decides which handler catches it;
- a cast or `instanceof` that the declared class does not answer;
- `sameClass` and the exact-class test an effect contract needs.

Anything the declared class does answer is still proved.

**Verification:**
- **Challenge fixture:** copied unchanged from the challenge stream (`lqvlvwsm`); the checker-side test from its README is added to `lib/tests/rule_countermodels.rs`.

**Reply:**

I fixed inbox item I010 and committed it as `twtuqvvr`, with 0 errors. Step 3 is still the next piece of work.

**The hole:** an effect contract could be proved by reading a `final` field on the receiver or an argument. The contract's proof builds those objects in a fresh state. A real caller may have built them in a different state, so the field can hold something the proof never saw. The challenge stream's two callers (`cc.Held#snapshotLevel` and `#scaledLevel`) were proved to return the level they were given, where a JVM returns 0.

**The fix:** inside an effect contract's proof, reading a final field of an object that existed before the call is now refused, and the refusal names the field. That is what the contract's own note already claimed it never read. The challenge stream offered a narrower alternative: keep the exemption for final fields set only from constructor parameters. I didn't take it, because it would need an analysis of the constructors and no setter the claim needs reads a final field.

**Still open:** ordinary lemmas (not effect contracts) can still read final fields. That belongs to the challenge stream's item 3, which wasn't in this inbox, so I left it alone.

**Verified:**
- I copied the challenge stream's fixture, README and JVM test unchanged. I also added its checker-side test, extended to require that the refusal names the field.
- With the refusal switched off, that test fails.
- The tests of everything I changed pass.

- Each write the stand-in makes now passes that same check first. Both examples are now refused, with the same reason as when the setter runs as written.
- A result proved with a write set now says it, for example "and writes nothing that was there before the call". Before, an empty write set over a static method left no trace in the result at all.

**Tests:**
- The challenge stream's fixture and its JVM test are copied unchanged.
- Its suggested test is added to `lib/tests/effect_countermodels.rs`. It also requires the contract to be proved and the refusal to name the write. With the fix removed, it fails on `Store.f`.
